extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP attorneys, in-house counsel evaluating §101 issues
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Alice/Mayo two-step framework (and related tests) to determine whether asserted patent claims are directed to an abstract idea and/or contain an inventive concept, using Federal Circuit and district-court holdings as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular configuration and method can defeat 'abstract idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that specify a particular configuration of sensors and a particular method of using raw sensor data to more accurately calculate position and orientation are not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims reciting an inertial tracking system with a particular configuration of inertial sensors and a particular method of using the raw data were held not abstract (Visual Memory v. NVIDIA). Anti-pattern: purely high‑level descriptions of tracking without particular sensor configuration or specific data‑processing steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological improvement in computer hardware/software weighs against abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to a technological improvement — e.g., an enhanced computer memory system using programmable operational characteristics configurable based on processor type — are not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat improvements to computer functioning (hardware or software) as non‑abstract. Example: enhanced memory configurable by processor type. Emphasize how claimed features improve the functioning of the computer rather than merely perform an abstract task on a generic computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-abstract improvement in computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effect a non-abstract improvement in computer functionality (rather than claiming the abstract idea generally) are patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims directed to computer security/monitoring systems that improve computer functionality were held eligible. Focus drafts on how the invention improves specific computer capabilities or fixes a computer‑specific problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims tied to improved user interfaces or small-screen functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improve the functioning of computers in specific contexts (for example, improved display interface for small screens) are not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: improved display interface for small screens (Core Wireless). Show how the claimed interface overcomes constraints of the device environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the claims as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The eligibility inquiry requires that the claims be read as a whole rather than dissected into isolated elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims for navigating three‑dimensional electronic spreadsheets were found non‑abstract when read as a whole. Anti-pattern: evaluating only individual steps in isolation and ignoring their combined contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic/recitation of routine steps indicates lack of inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite only generic steps (e.g., creating a base version, creating a new version, and determining changes) and nothing more are likely to lack an inventive concept and be ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: spreadsheet change‑tracking claims were ineligible for reciting only generic versioning steps. Guidance: include non‑generic elements or show how the steps are tied to a specific technological implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the patent's 'claimed advance' at Alice step one
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, courts examine the patent's 'claimed advance' to determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea or to a specific technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ancora — courts look to what the patent asserts it advances. Drafting tip: clearly state the claimed advance in the specification and claims to frame step‑one analysis favorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software can constitute non-abstract computer improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Software that effects a technological improvement to computer technology can render claims non-abstract; improvements need not be hardware‑only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: software that changes computer behavior (Ancora) was recognized as capable of improving computer technology. Emphasize how software elements materially change computer operation or solve a computer‑specific problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap between step one and step two considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts recognize overlaps between Alice step one (directed to) and step two (inventive concept) considerations; some factual questions relevant to step two may influence step one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: court notes overlaps and remands when factual issues on inventive concept exist (Data Engine). Be prepared to present factual record on whether claim limitations are routine or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine‑or‑transformation (MOT) test remains relevant in some contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if claims are argued to be abstract, satisfying the machine‑or‑transformation test (e.g., where a computer plays a significant role in real‑time data capture/transmission) can support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims involving real‑time data capture/transmission satisfied MOT arguments (Helios). Use evidence showing specific machine involvement or a transformation of an article into a different state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowly defined algorithms tied to specific processes can be inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms, even if mathematical, that are narrowly defined and tied to a specific process or error‑correction technique can constitute meaningful limitations representing a specific inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: encoding/decoding data tied to an error correction process (Caltech v. Hughes). Draft to show narrow definition and concrete application of algorithms in a technical process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting claims to a particular technological field supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims limited to a particular technological field or particular form of a technology (e.g., electronic trading with an intuitive grid display) can be not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: click‑based trading limited to electronic trading with a technological improvement was eligible. Avoid overbroad functional language that would cover non‑technological implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and convincing evidence standard for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts apply the clear and convincing evidence standard to a party seeking to establish patent invalidity for ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: defendant failed to establish ineligibility by clear and convincing evidence (Ameritox). Litigation guidance: preserve evidence and fact record showing non‑conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims 'rooted in computer technology' to overcome internet-centric problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims rooted in computer/network technology that address problems specifically arising in the Internet or computer context are likely eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: solutions rooted in computer technology to overcome Internet‑centric problems (business intelligence automatic agent, remote access portal). Show how the claimed features are necessarily tied to computer/network constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, non‑generic devices/systems as meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting particular non‑generic devices or trusted systems (e.g., a repository that is a 'trusted system' using digital certificates) can supply an inventive concept and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: digital rights management claims requiring a 'trusted system' and digital certificates. Anti-pattern: reciting a generic 'computer' or 'server' without specific structure or function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical device/layout claims are typically not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to physical layouts or tangible machine configurations (e.g., physical memory card layouts enabling slimmer profile or more chips) are generally not directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: semiconductor memory card physical layouts held eligible. Emphasize tangible, physical characteristics and how they achieve a technical result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a mathematical formula in a novel technical way
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a mathematical formula in a novel technical manner to define physical parameters (e.g., spacing between subcarriers) can render claims eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: novel application of mathematical formula to spacing in bandlimited channels (paging carrier case). Show how math is applied to solve a technical engineering problem rather than claiming the formula itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims solving multiple technical problems with technical solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that address multiple technical problems in a field with corresponding technical solutions indicate eligibility and inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: vehicle radar claims solving at least three technical problems in blind‑spot detection. Identify each technical problem and the claimed technical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifying how the Internet/computer functions can be an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that modify the way the Internet or computer systems function (e.g., using client identity to control access over an untrusted network) can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using identity associated with client computer to control access was held to modify Internet functioning and be inventive. Draft to show systemic change to network behavior, not mere data manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming preemption of every application of an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be so broad as to preempt all applications of an abstract idea; narrowly claiming a particular way of performing a function helps eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim covering only one specific way to calculate an average power did not attempt to preempt every application. Draft claims to carve out a particular implementation rather than monopolize a concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity that places meaningful boundaries on the inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims described with particular steps and parameter determination that place meaningful boundaries are less likely to be abstract and more likely to have an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: image scanning claims that determine parameters and apply them to operate a scanner; court found sufficient specificity. Include concrete parameter values/relationships and how they are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination of steps can supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered combination of steps that together produce a technological improvement (e.g., faster access to electronic pictorial data) can constitute an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'ordered combination' of steps in geographic data display allowed faster access and was eligibility‑supporting. Emphasize the sequence and interaction among limitations, not just each in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that 'do more' than an analog counterpart can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that do more than a traditional analog counterpart (e.g., provide proof of delivery and content, not just proof of mailing) may avoid being abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: electronic message delivery claims providing proof of delivery and content. Show additional technical functionality uniquely enabled by the electronic implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem specifically arising in the technological realm indicates eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that address problems that specifically arise in the realm of computers/networks (not long‑prevalent human processes) are more likely to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims reducing host processing demand or addressing network congestion in defined environments. Identify why the problem is intrinsic to the technology and how the claim addresses it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual questions regarding conventionality/inventive concept may require remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are underlying factual disputes (e.g., whether limitations are conventional or provide an inventive concept), courts may remand to the district court rather than resolve §101 on the pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Data Engine remanded some claims because of factual questions. Build factual record (expert declarations, prior art comparisons) to counter assertions of conventionality.
